analysis.one_liner: Gives the Agriculture Secretary power to order recalls of contaminated meat and poultry and fine violators.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee from January 1999 until the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law at the time, the federal government could not force a meat or poultry company to pull contaminated product off store shelves — it could only ask, and companies often negotiated. This bill would have required companies to report adulterated product, given the Agriculture Secretary authority to order mandatory recalls and halt distribution, allowed inspectors to be pulled from repeat-offender plants, and added civil fines of up to $100,000 per violation. It was introduced by Senator Tom Harkin with eight Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Agriculture Committee, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of meat and poultry — essentially everyone — who would be warned faster when E. coli, Salmonella, or other contamination reaches the food supply, and who would benefit from stronger enforcement against plants with repeated violations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who eats meat or poultry

how_it_helps.text: Requires any business handling meat or poultry to notify the Agriculture Secretary immediately if it has reason to believe the product is adulterated or misbranded [S3].
Lets the Secretary order companies to stop distributing and recall contaminated product when they will not do it voluntarily, instead of relying on requests [S2] [S3].
Lets the Secretary withdraw inspectors from plants with willful or repeated violations, which halts a plant's ability to sell product across state lines [S3].
Adds civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counting as a separate offense, collected through the Attorney General if unpaid [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processing companies, which would bear the cost of recalls, notification, and potential fines; some of those costs could be passed to consumers in meat prices. Small plants would be subject to the same penalties as large ones, though the bill tells the Secretary to weigh business size when setting fine amounts.

drawbacks.text: Recalls are expensive, and mandatory recall authority backed by $100,000-per-violation-per-day fines would impose significant costs on processors, particularly smaller plants [S3].

The bill gives the Secretary very broad discretion over when a product threatens public health and how recalls proceed, with limited judicial review after the fact, which processors and some lawmakers viewed as excessive regulatory power [S3].
The industry already had strong incentives to recall voluntarily to limit its own liability; opponents argued a mandatory regime adds bureaucracy without much added safety [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real: mandatory recall authority would have closed a gap where the government could only ask companies to pull contaminated meat, and faster removal of tainted product prevents illness. The costs fall on processors and potentially on meat prices, and the fine structure is blunt, though it directs regulators to account for business size. On balance the bill addressed a genuine public-health gap with a tool the industry had long resisted.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on January 19, 1999, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors including Senator Daschle [S1] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
The bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors are better off: without the bill, they faced no mandatory recall orders, no civil penalties, and no threat of inspectors being pulled from repeat-violation plants. Consumers kept a system where recalls were voluntary and negotiable.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFER Meat and Poultry Act to create mandatory recall authority and civil penalties for adulterated meat and poultry.

for.name: Sens. Daschle, Johnson, Mikulski, Kennedy, Torricelli, Durbin, Leahy, and Boxer

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress; it died in committee.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory recall authority and civil penalties during the period when Congress considered meat safety legislation; Congress did not enact such authority during the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; the Republican-controlled Senate Agriculture Committee never acted on the bill, and there was no floor vote to measure bipartisan support.

industries.note: The bill would have made them report contamination, obey mandatory recall orders, and face fines up to $100,000 per violation per day. Their interest in avoiding recalls and fines runs against consumers' interest in tainted product being pulled quickly. The bill never passed, so their position under the old voluntary-recall system was preserved.

Notified handlers would have been required to immediately stop distribution of contaminated product, adding compliance burden, but faster recalls would reduce their exposure to selling tainted goods. Secondary to the processors' stake.
